strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: adding music conditioning to strong text-to-video diffusion models for dance video generation, while retaining prompt control over dancer appearance, scene, and style.

The proposed system is practical and relatively lightweight: frozen Mochi backbone, Wav2Vec audio features, zero-initialized music-video cross-attention, and LoRA adaptation trained in about 20 hours on one A100. Avoiding motion capture or reconstructed skeleton supervision is an appealing design choice.

The method is clearly described at a high level, with reasonable component motivations: gradual audio injection via zero-initialized cross-attention, higher-rank LoRA for spatiotemporal adaptation, beta-to-uniform noise scheduling, caption diversification, and selected adapter layers.

The experimental section includes relevant ablations over the proposed components. The full model usually gives the best aggregate score, and qualitative figures suggest better visual quality than MM-Diffusion and retained prompt adherence compared with the base Mochi model.
The work has potential practical value for creative tools because it combines music responsiveness and text-driven scene/style control in a single video generation pipeline.
weaknesses: The main evidence is not strong enough to fully support the central claim of music-synchronized dance generation. Quantitative evaluation relies almost entirely on VideoLLaMA/Video-LLM ratings for beat alignment, style alignment, movement realism, and prompt satisfaction, but the paper does not validate that these ratings correlate with human judgment or with objective audio-motion synchronization measures.

There is no human user study, no standard beat-alignment metric, no motion/audio correlation analysis, no statistical significance or variance, and only limited information about the number and diversity of generated samples beyond the 10 music tracks x 10 prompts setup. This is a serious limitation because the key contribution is perceptual and temporal.

The baselines are not fully convincing. Mochi is a text-only video model and cannot use music, while MM-Diffusion is an older general audio-video diffusion baseline with much lower visual quality and limited style control. The paper does not compare against recent music-to-dance or human animation systems in a way that isolates music responsiveness, even if those methods output motion/skeletons rather than final video.

Several headline generalization claims are supported only qualitatively: longer videos, group choreography, unseen K-pop-like music, speed control, and in-the-wild music examples. The figures are encouraging but appear too sparse to establish robust generalization rather than selected examples.

The technical novelty is moderate. Zero-initialized cross-attention, LoRA-based adaptation, and noise-schedule modifications are reasonable engineering choices, but each is close to established adaptation practice; the paper would be stronger with deeper analysis of why these components specifically improve music-motion synchronization.

The layer selection criterion is weakly justified: choosing layers based on imaging/aesthetic quality from STG/VBench does not directly measure audio conditioning or dance synchronization, and the relationship between this proxy and the target task remains unclear.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The YouTube training data collection, filtering, licensing, exact clip list, captioning details, and evaluation prompts/models are only partially specified; the abstract mentions project/code availability but the visible manuscript does not provide an actual accessible link.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and useful problem: adding music conditioning to pretrained text-to-video diffusion models for dance video generation, while retaining text control over scene, subject, and style.

The proposed system is reasonably simple and practical: zero-initialized audio-video cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, and selective layer insertion are plausible engineering choices that could be useful for adapting large video generators without full retraining.

The manuscript includes component ablations over ZICA layer selection, LoRA rank, beta-uniform scheduling, and feature-addition conditioning, which at least attempts to isolate the contribution of the proposed design choices.

Using both AIST and additional in-the-wild dance videos is sensible for reducing overfitting to studio data, and the paper reports implementation details such as training steps, GPU, learning rate, audio encoder, LoRA rank, and guidance scale.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not adequately support the central claim that the generated motion is synchronized to music. The main quantitative evaluation relies almost entirely on VideoLLaMA-style 0-10 judgments, with no validation that this evaluator reliably measures beat alignment, dance style alignment, or choreographic quality. There is no human study, no correlation analysis, no beat/motion onset metric, and no objective audio-motion synchronization measure.

The comparison protocol is weak and potentially unfair. MM-Diffusion is an older general audio-video model rather than a strong music-to-dance or current video-generation baseline, and Mochi cannot hear audio, so the baselines do not convincingly establish that MusicInfuser is strong relative to relevant alternatives. The paper also omits comparisons to motion-conditioned dance generation pipelines followed by rendering/animation, or newer human video/audio-driven methods except in a brief concurrent-work discussion.

Many key results are qualitative and depend on external videos/project-page inspection. The PDF itself repeatedly states that beat/style alignment is clearer on the project page, while static frame strips cannot substantiate synchronization. Claims about in-the-wild music, longer generation, group choreography, diversity, and difficulty control are demonstrated mostly with selected examples rather than systematic evaluation.

The proposed technical novelties are incremental and not deeply justified. Zero-initialized cross-attention and LoRA adaptation are standard adaptation ideas; the HR-LoRA motivation using homography degrees of freedom is hand-wavy; and the layer selection criterion appears based on STG imaging/aesthetic scores rather than a principled measure of audio-conditioning utility. The ablation gains are small and sometimes mixed, e.g. removing beta-uniform improves style and beat alignment in Table 4 while the text claims it improves body representation.

The evaluation tables are difficult to interpret because the Video-LLM scores are treated as authoritative despite obvious limitations. For example, ground-truth AIST scores are only modestly above generated outputs on dance quality, and MusicInfuser nearly matches or exceeds real data on some subjective dimensions, which raises concerns about metric calibration.

The dataset and training details are incomplete for reproducibility. The YouTube data collection procedure, filtering, licenses, clip selection criteria, audio preprocessing, exact selected ZICA layers, caption replacement probability, beta decay schedule, train/test contamination safeguards for YouTube data, and evaluation sampling protocol are under-specified.

The paper overstates generalization. Testing on a few SUNO or TikTok tracks and showing selected frame strips is not sufficient to conclude generalization to unseen music categories, longer videos, or group choreography, especially since the training already includes diverse YouTube dance videos.

Clarity and polish are below the expected standard in places. There are visible formatting/text issues, cramped tables, typos, and a blank project/code URL in the extracted manuscript. More importantly, the narrative sometimes turns limitations of the evidence into strong claims rather than clearly separating demonstrated results from anecdotal examples.

strengths: The paper addresses an appealing and timely problem: adding music conditioning to a strong text-to-video diffusion model for dance generation while preserving text prompt control. The framing is useful because it avoids requiring motion-capture data and leverages existing video priors rather than training a large joint audio-video model from scratch.

The method is technically sensible and fairly well motivated. Zero-initialized music-video cross-attention is a reasonable way to introduce audio conditioning without immediately disrupting the base model, and the combination with higher-rank LoRA, beta-uniform noise scheduling, caption diversification, and selective layer insertion forms a coherent adaptation recipe.

The empirical results are encouraging. MusicInfuser improves over MM-Diffusion and the Mochi base model on the reported VideoLLaMA-based dance quality average, with especially strong beat alignment and movement realism, while retaining competitive video quality and prompt alignment. The ablation table supports the contribution of the proposed components, with the full model obtaining the best overall score.

The paper shows several useful capabilities beyond the core benchmark, including prompt-controlled scene/style changes, different dancer counts, speed responsiveness under tempo changes, longer generation than training clips, diverse outputs under different seeds, and qualitative generalization to out-of-distribution music.

The manuscript is generally clear and reproducibility is better than average in several respects: it reports base model, audio encoder, LoRA rank, learning rate, training steps, GPU budget, dataset mixture, AIST split protocol, evaluation prompts, and VideoLLaMA query templates.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies heavily on Video-LLM scores, and the paper does not sufficiently validate that these scores correlate with human judgments for beat synchronization, dance naturalness, or prompt satisfaction. This is particularly important because the main claims concern music-motion alignment, where frame-only figures and automated ratings may miss temporal artifacts.

Baselines are limited. The comparison to MM-Diffusion is relevant but not very strong for modern controllable human/dance generation, and the paper does not quantitatively compare against recent music-to-dance or human animation systems in a way that separates choreography quality, visual realism, and text controllability. Some prior methods may output motion rather than video, but the paper could still include converted/rendered comparisons or explain the incompatibility more rigorously.

Several generalization claims are supported mainly by qualitative examples. The K-pop/SUNO, TikTok, group-dancer, and longer-video results are interesting, but there is no systematic quantitative evaluation for these settings, no failure-rate reporting, and no analysis of whether the model truly follows unseen musical structure rather than producing plausible generic dance motion.

The ablation evidence is useful but the margins are modest and sometimes mixed. For example, removing beta-uniform scheduling improves style and beat alignment in Table 4 while hurting body representation/video quality, and the paper does not deeply analyze these tradeoffs or report variance/significance across seeds or music tracks.

Reproducibility is still incomplete for the most important data-dependent pieces. The YouTube in-the-wild dataset collection, filtering, captions, exact selected ZICA layers, and project/code availability are not fully specified in the manuscript, making it difficult to reproduce the training corpus and layer selection procedure exactly.

The method inherits substantial limitations from the base T2V model, including body-part distortions, face/finger failures, silhouette confusion, and potential identity/body inconsistency during fast motion. The paper acknowledges these issues, but they are central for a dance-video generation system and are not quantified.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: adding music responsiveness to strong text-to-video diffusion models for dance generation while retaining prompt control. The proposed system is practically appealing because it avoids motion-capture or skeleton intermediates and reports single-A100 training within about 20 hours.

The method is coherent and well motivated. Zero-initialized audio cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, selective layer insertion, and the beta-to-uniform noise schedule form a plausible recipe for preserving the pretrained video prior while introducing audio conditioning.

The paper provides several useful ablations. Tables 1, 5, and 6 compare layer selection strategies, all-layer adaptation, feature addition, no zero initialization, no LoRA, no beta-uniform schedule, and no in-the-wild data. These studies support the claim that the full design is better than several simple alternatives.

Qualitative examples cover diverse prompts, multiple dancers, tempo changes, longer generation, unseen subjects, and in-the-wild music. These examples make the potential usefulness of the approach clear, especially for controllable dance video synthesis.

The authors include both automatic evaluation and a human A/B study, and the supplement reports evaluation prompts, test music codes, prompt templates, and failure cases, which improves transparency relative to many video generation papers.
weaknesses: The evaluation evidence is not strong enough to fully support the broad claims. Most quantitative results rely on Video-LLM scores from Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2. These models are not established as reliable judges of fine-grained beat synchronization, body realism, or choreography quality, and some scores look suspicious, e.g. a body representation score of 10.00 in Table 1 and generated choreography/complexity exceeding ground-truth AIST in Table 2.

The human evaluation is limited in scope. It reports A/B preferences against MM-Diffusion only, with 33 participants, but does not compare against recent dance-generation or human-animation systems in a way that would establish the method’s position relative to the strongest alternatives. The protocol details are sparse: number of clips, randomization, statistical uncertainty, and participant expertise are not sufficiently clear in the main evidence.

Baselines are somewhat weak or mismatched. MM-Diffusion is a general audio-video diffusion model and Mochi is a text-to-video baseline without music conditioning; neither is a strong dedicated music-to-dance video baseline. Skeleton methods are discussed as limited, but the paper does not provide a careful comparison that separates motion quality from rendering quality or evaluates whether skeleton-conditioned video rendering would be competitive.

Several key claims are mainly qualitative: generalization to SUNO-generated music, longer 9-second clips, animal subjects, tempo control, and multiple dancers are shown through figures and supplementary video rather than systematic metrics. These are interesting capabilities, but the evidence does not establish their robustness.

The technical novelty is useful but moderate. Zero-initialized adapters/cross-attention, LoRA, audio encoders, and curriculum-like noise scheduling are all familiar ingredients. The layer adaptability criterion is the most distinctive part, but it is only indirectly justified by VBench-like imaging/aesthetic scores and its relationship to audio-motion controllability is not rigorously established.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some training details, dataset sizes, and prompts, but the in-the-wild YouTube data collection is not specified in enough detail to reproduce, the selected layer list is not explicitly enumerated, and there is no clear code/model/data release statement. Since the method depends on private or hard-to-recreate web video mixtures and Video-LLM evaluation, independent verification may be difficult.

The presentation occasionally overclaims. Phrases such as “text-to-video models already know how to dance” and claims of closing the gap between music and dance are stronger than the demonstrated evidence. The paper would be more convincing if it framed the contribution as a promising adaptation strategy rather than a broadly validated solution.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: adding music responsiveness to strong text-to-video diffusion models for dance generation, while retaining text control over appearance, scene, and style.

The proposed system is practically motivated. Sparse zero-initialized audio cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, and a single-GPU training recipe are potentially useful for adapting large video diffusion models without full retraining.

The manuscript includes several relevant ablations: layer placement, all-layer adaptation, feature addition, beta-uniform scheduling, zero initialization, LoRA variants, and in-the-wild data. These make an effort to separate the contributions of the engineering choices.
Qualitative examples suggest that the method can preserve text-conditioned visual diversity and produce more plausible videos than an older audio-video diffusion baseline in some cases.
weaknesses: The evidence for the central claims is not strong enough. The main quantitative evaluation relies heavily on Video-LLM scores from Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2 for beat alignment, motion realism, choreography complexity, and video quality. These are not established objective measures for music-dance synchronization, and the paper provides only limited validation beyond a coarse human preference study.

The reported gains over the strongest relevant baselines are small or ambiguous. Compared with Mochi, MusicInfuser improves dance quality from 7.70 to 7.95 and video quality from 8.78 to 8.95, while body representation drops from 7.47 to 7.16. Prompt alignment improves only 8.86 to 8.96. These margins are hard to interpret without variance, significance testing, or stronger independent metrics.

The baseline set is weak for the stated contribution. MM-Diffusion is an older general audio-video model and is not a strong contemporary dance-video or human-animation baseline. Comparisons to skeleton-based methods such as EDGE are mostly qualitative or indirect, and the paper does not adequately compare against recent audio-conditioned human video generation or motion-conditioned video methods.

The layer-adaptability criterion is under-justified. It selects layers using improvements in video imaging/aesthetic quality under skip guidance, but the desired adaptation target is audio-conditioned dance synchronization. The connection between this score and optimal layers for music-motion conditioning is asserted rather than convincingly demonstrated.

Several claimed generalization results are mainly qualitative: unseen subjects, animals, synthetic K-pop music, tempo changes, and longer 9-second videos. These are interesting demonstrations, but the paper does not provide rigorous evaluation of synchronization, identity consistency, temporal drift, or failure frequency under these settings.

The human evaluation is insufficiently specified and too narrow. The paper reports 33 participants and strong preference over MM-Diffusion, but does not clearly report the number of evaluated videos per comparison, statistical confidence, participant screening, randomization details, or comparisons against Mochi and other relevant baselines.

Originality is moderate rather than compelling. Zero-initialized cross-attention, LoRA adaptation, Wav2Vec conditioning, prompt diversification, and curriculum-like noise scheduling are reasonable engineering choices, but the paper’s novelty rests on combining known mechanisms with a layer-selection heuristic whose theoretical and empirical support is limited.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details about the 15,799 YouTube clips, playlist identities, filtering, audio-video synchronization, preprocessing, exact selected layers, full training settings, and evaluation implementation are missing or only lightly described. This makes the results difficult to reproduce or audit.

The manuscript overstates conclusions relative to the evidence, e.g. claims of closing the gap between music and dance, robust generalization, and listening capability are stronger than what the experiments establish. The limitations section acknowledges inherited artifacts, body-part merging, and face/finger failures, but these issues are not quantitatively characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses a compelling and timely problem: adapting pretrained text-to-video diffusion models so generated dance videos respond to a specified music track while retaining prompt control. This is a useful direction because it bypasses skeleton or motion-capture intermediates and leverages strong video priors.

The proposed adaptation strategy is technically sensible. Zero-initialized cross-attention for audio conditioning, LoRA-based adaptation, and the beta-to-uniform noise schedule are well motivated for preserving the base model while adding a new modality.

The layer-wise adaptability criterion is an interesting contribution. Selecting 16 of 48 DiT layers using a guidance-inspired positive influence score is more original than simply adding audio adapters everywhere, and the ablations show consistent gains over all-layer, early/middle/late, and evenly distributed adapter placement.

The experimental results are encouraging. MusicInfuser improves over MM-Diffusion and Mochi on most reported dance/video quality metrics, and the ablations support the main design choices. Human A/B evaluation also strongly favors the proposed method over MM-Diffusion across video quality, music-dance alignment, motion realism, and choreography complexity.

The method appears practically useful: training is reported to fit on a single A100 in about 20 hours, uses existing dance videos rather than mocap, supports text control, and demonstrates qualitative generalization to longer clips, unseen music, varied scenes, and nonhuman subjects.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies heavily on Video-LLM scoring with Qwen3-Omni and VideoLLaMA 2. Although the authors include a human study, the paper does not provide enough statistical detail, variance, confidence intervals, or correlation analysis to fully establish these automatic metrics as reliable for fine-grained music-dance synchronization.

The comparison set is somewhat limited for the main quantitative claims. The paper compares mainly to MM-Diffusion and Mochi, while several music-to-dance and human animation methods are discussed but not quantitatively compared in a way that isolates dance synchronization, realism, or controllability across comparable settings.

Some reported gains are modest or mixed. For example, MusicInfuser is below ground truth on movement realism and video quality, below Mochi on body representation and aesthetic quality in some tables, and the choreography complexity numbers are not dramatically higher. The paper is still strong, but the claims of broad superiority should be phrased carefully.

The layer adaptability metric is appealing but not fully validated as a general principle. It is selected using imaging quality from the base model, yet the target task is audio-motion alignment; the paper would be stronger with deeper analysis of why those layers are best for music conditioning and whether the selected layers transfer across base models or datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details about the in-the-wild YouTube dataset, filtering, licensing, exact preprocessing, model release, and whether code/checkpoints will be available are not sufficiently specified. Since the method depends on a large pretrained video model and collected web videos, this affects independent reproduction.

The qualitative claims about longer-video generation, unseen music categories, speed control, and unusual subjects are visually interesting but mostly anecdotal. More systematic evaluation of temporal drift, beat alignment over longer horizons, and failure frequency would make these claims more convincing.
